title: Electromechanical behavior in damage detection of self-sensing cementitious composites containing carbon nanotubes and polypropylene fibers
abstract: Abstract This study investigates the self-sensing capabilities of cement pastes containing multi-walled carbon nanotubes (CNT) and polypropylene (PP) fibers. The primary objective is to evaluate the variations in the electrical properties of the composite as a function of damage initiation. Tensile splitting tests were employed as a controlled damage induction method, ensuring the formation of a single, well-defined, and localized crack. This experimental approach allows for a precise correlation between structural damage and corresponding alterations in electrical resistivity. Specimens were prepared with five different CNT concentrations, ranging from 0.00% to 1.00%, and a fixed 0.50% content of PP fibers by volume of cement paste. Electrical resistivity measurements identified the percolation threshold at 0.12% CNT, with the material entering the stable conduction zone between 0.50% and 0.75% CNT. The 0.50% CNT concentration, which is situated within the transition zone, yielded the highest sensitivity to cracking, with the fractional change in resistivity (FCR) reaching values between 125% and 500% at the moment of failure. While higher CNT concentrations (0.75% and 1.00%) provided superior electrical conductivity, they exhibited less sensitivity due to their denser conductive networks. In contrast, lower concentrations proved ineffective for damage detection. This research demonstrates that the exceptional electrical properties of CNT, combined with the crack-bridging effect of PP fibers, create a multifunctional synergistic composite. This combination yields both high electromechanical sensitivity and crack control, demonstrating the viability of this smart material as an intrinsic sensor for Structural Health Monitoring in civil infrastructure.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The integration of Structural Health Monitoring (SHM) into civil engineering structures has traditionally relied on the use of external sensors for non-destructive techniques, which often face durability issues and limited spatial coverage [ 1 ,  2 ]. Recently, the development of Self-sensing Cementitious Composites (SSCC) has emerged, enabling the material itself to act as an intrinsic sensor [ 3 ,  4 ] with the potential to assess its entire domain. This functional capability often arises from the piezoresistive effect, where electrical properties (conductivity and resistivity) fluctuate in response to mechanical strain [ 5 ,  6 ,  7 ,  8 – 9 ]. By incorporating conductive fillers, such as carbon nanotubes (CNT), into the cementitious matrix, an internal conductive network is established [ 3 ,  10 ] enhancing its sensitivity to these changes. Compared to other carbon-based materials like carbon black, carbon fibers, or graphene, CNT offer distinct advantages, including an exceptionally low percolation threshold and reversible piezoresistive sensitivity [ 11 ,  12 – 13 ]. Within this pathway, electrical transport occurs not only through direct physical contact, but also via tunneling conduction across thin layers of the hydration products of the cement paste between CNT particles [ 5 ,  14 ]. Consequently, the composite is capable of monitoring its own deformation and structural response through variations in electrical resistance [ 9 ,  15 ]. However, the performance of these smart materials is generally highly sensitive to the dosage and dispersion quality of the functional fillers [ 16 ,  17 ].

One major issue associated with the use of carbon nanotubes is their tendency to agglomerate. Factors such as small particle size and high surface area promote strong van der Waals forces which, combined with the hydrophobic nature of this nanomaterial, present a significant challenge for its incorporation into cement composites [ 12 ,  18 ,  19 ]. Effectively dispersing nanomaterials is essential to achieve enhanced and consistent performance [ 20 ]. Therefore, to prevent agglomeration, various methodologies have been studied for dispersing CNT in aqueous solutions, including mechanical and chemical methods [ 16 ,  19 ,  21 ,  22 – 23 ]. While a well-dispersed CNT network ensures reversible piezoresistive behavior within the elastic regime, the onset of cracking triggers a disruption of these conductive pathways [ 24 ,  25 – 26 ]. This structural damage manifests as an immediate and sharp increase in electrical resistance, the magnitude of which is governed by the concentration of the functional fillers [ 9 ,  17 ]. Furthermore, factors such as polarization can introduce significant drift into electrical measurements, particularly under direct current (DC), requiring robust data acquisition strategies [ 6 ,  8 ,  27 ].

The incorporation of CNT also promotes nucleation effects that optimize the pore structure, resulting in better control over the development of submicron cracks within the composite [ 24 ]. Nevertheless, the construction industry faces a critical challenge in mitigating the degradation of concrete structures caused by larger-scale cracks. To overcome this limitation, improve mechanical performance, and ensure the durability and extended service life of these systems, the introduction of polymeric fiber reinforcement, such as Polypropylene (PP) fibers, represents an effective strategy to control crack propagation and ensure structural integrity [ 28 ]. Due to their low cost and favorable mechanical properties, such as ductility and anchoring, PP fibers stand out as an effective admixture for cement-based materials. Their high melting point ensures greater thermal stability than many alternative polymer reinforcements, and their non-corrosive nature enhances long-term durability [ 29 ,  30 ]. Additionally, they are chemically inert, remaining stable in both the alkaline environment of cementitious matrices as well as in aggressive acidic environments [ 31 ]. Moreover, the application of hybrid fibers, such as carbon nanotubes and PP fibers, has been found to be more effective than the use of a single type of fiber in terms of mechanical performance [ 32 ]. While non-conductive fibers do not actively participate in electron transport, their crack-bridging capability prevents abrupt macroscopic failures where CNT reach their limits. This allows the internal CNT network to undergo a progressive, rather than instantaneous, disruption. Consequently, the composite can continuously register damage evolution and maintain a stable electrical signal [ 33 ].

While the individual benefits of CNT in enhancing electrical conductivity and PP fibers enhancing ductility and crack control are established, their synergistic electromechanical behavior requires further investigation to optimize their application as SSCC. In this context, the present study evaluates this combined performance of cement composites reinforced with CNT and PP fibers. The main focus of this research is to identify the critical range of CNT concentrations where the material can effectively detect structural damage through electrical resistivity measurements during tensile splitting tests. Using a constant DC voltage source and an optimized data acquisition system, this study identifies the specific percolation and conduction thresholds, determining where the fractional change in resistivity (FCR) most accurately reflects the onset of the first crack. This approach isolates the electromechanical response of a single-crack initiation to establish the precise electrical signal of these composites. These results contribute to a deeper understanding of how hybrid CNT-fiber systems can provide a reliable, intrinsic monitoring solution for modern engineering applications.

sections.heading: Materials
paragraphs: Cement/PP/CNT composites were produced using a high early-strength Portland cement (CP-V ARI), equivalent to ASTM C150 Type III, from Lafarge-Holcim (Rio de Janeiro, Brazil). Multi-walled carbon nanotubes NC700 (purity of 90% and surface area between 250 and 300 m²/g) produced by Nanocyl S.A. (Sambreville, Belgium) and a second-generation naphthalene-based superplasticizer, MasterRheobuild 1000 (SP 1 ) with a solids content of 40.5% was used for CNT dispersion procedures. Viscosity-modifying agent (VMA), MasterMatrix UW410, deionized water, and the superplasticizer Glenium 51 (SP 2 ) were used. Finally, polypropylene fibers with a 12 μm diameter, 6 mm length, and relative density 0.91 g/cm 3  were incorporated for crack opening control.

sections.heading: Materials characterization
paragraphs: The chemical composition of the cement was obtained by X-ray fluorescence (XRF) spectroscopy using a Shimadzu EDX-720 spectrometer equipped with a rhodium tube and a liquid nitrogen-cooled silicon detector. The XRF results were normalized based on loss on ignition (LOI), which was determined at 950 °C with a 15-minute residence time in a muffle furnace programmed at a heating rate of 10 °C/min. Carbon nanotubes were characterized using transmission electron microscopy (TEM), in bright-field mode, at an acceleration of 75 kV and a magnification of 270,000x. Prior to imaging, the CNT dispersion was deposited onto a copper grid and dried in a desiccator at room temperature.

sections.heading: CNT dispersion
paragraphs: This study used a superplasticizer as a chemical dispersant, combined with mechanical mixing provided by an ultrasonic processor. The amount of CNT used was 2% by mass, with a CNT: dispersant solids ratio of 1:1, while the remainder of the solution consists of deionized water, as reported in [ 34 ]. The SP 1  was first stirred in deionized water prior to the incorporation of the carbon nanotubes. After adding the nanoparticles in three intervals and mixing them manually with a glass rod, the suspension underwent 10 sonication cycles at an average energy of 110 J/g of dispersion. The sonication was performed using a Sonics Vibra-Cell VCX 500 ultrasonic processor, set to a 40% amplitude, in on/off pulses at 20-second intervals, spaced one minute apart to prevent overheating. To obtain the required amount of CNT content for the composites, 10 separate dispersions were prepared, producing about 25 g each.

The Ocean Optics Flame-Chem-UV-Vis benchtop spectrophotometer was used to perform UV-Vis spectroscopy analyses to evaluate the quality of the nanoparticle dispersions. Before and after the procedure, an aliquot of the CNT suspension was diluted with deionized water at a 1:2000 ratio in a volumetric flask. Subsequently, the solution was transferred to a polystyrene cuvette with a 10 mm path length for the test. For the first dispersion (D1), this procedure was repeated to each of the 10 cycles. For the remaining 9 dispersions (D2 to D10) the UV-Vis spectroscopy was performed in the last cycle. Moreover, the final solid content was quantified by mass loss analysis. For this, a Shimadzu MOC63u moisture balance was used. The procedure consists of placing 1 g of the dispersion on the moisture balance, which is programmed to initially heat to 200 °C and then automatically decrease to 100 °C as soon as the variation in moisture loss between measurements taken every 30 s is less than 0.5%. The test continues until the sample reaches a constant mass. The weight of solids must also account for the particles present in the dispersant used. To ensure the reliability of the results, the experiment was performed three times.

sections.heading: Mixing procedure and sample preparation
paragraphs: The cement/PP/CNT specimens were prepared by incorporating dispersed CNT at concentrations of 0.00%, 0.25%, 0.50%, 0.75%, and 1.00% by mass of cement, utilizing a fixed water-to-cement (w/c) ratio of 0.5. This value was established as the minimum achievable limit due to the water content already present within the CNT dispersion. The mixing procedure began by homogenizing the water and the pre-dispersed CNT solution for 1 min using a glass rod, followed by the sequential introduction of 0.50% of VMA and cement powder in three parts. To control crack opening in tensile splitting tests, PP fibers were added in intervals to a total concentration of 0.50% by volume of cement paste. Due to the high viscosity of the resulting composite, Glenium 51 superplasticizer (SP 2 ) was introduced in variable concentrations to achieve similar consistency for all compositions. After 8 min of manual mixing to ensure homogeneity, a mechanical stirrer was used for two minutes at a velocity of 2500 rpm. Table  1  summarizes the mix proportions used in this study.

Table 1 Mix proportions of cement/PP/CNT samples Cement (%) CNT (%) SP 1  solids (%) SP 2  (%) PP fibers (%) VMA (%) w/c 0.00CNT 100.00 0.00 0.00 0.00 0.50 0.50 0.50 0.25CNT 0.25 0.25 0.45 0.50CNT 0.50 0.50 1.27 0.75CNT 0.75 0.75 1.27 1.00CNT 1.00 1.00 1.27

The fresh paste was cast into cylindrical bronze molds (50 mm in diameter and 25 mm in height) with a soldered pair of V-shaped notches (90º angle), using a glass rod for compaction to mitigate air voids. During this stage, two 15 × 40 mm copper electrodes were inserted into the matrix to ensure electrical contact. To prevent moisture evaporation, samples were hermetically sealed and subjected to thermal curing at 60 °C for 7 days. In the hardened state, two additional pairs of 2 mm wide notches were cut with a saw to induce a single, linear crack [ 35 ]. The representation of all mixing procedures and sample preparation is illustrated in Fig.  1 . Finally, to avoid moisture effects on electrical measurements, the samples were dried at 40 °C until constant mass and cooled in a desiccator for 24 h before the test to prevent temperature effects. This approach isolates the intrinsic sensing capability of the CNT network from ionic conduction.
Fig. 1 Illustration of mixing procedure and cement/PP/CNT samples preparation

sections.heading: Electromechanical test
paragraphs: Tensile splitting tests were selected to evaluate the correlation between mechanical performance and electrical signals. This setup ensures the formation of a controlled, linear crack path directly between the electrodes. The localized damage propagation, guided by the induced notches in the cement/PP/CNT samples, allows for a precise correlation between the exact crack opening and the disruption of the conductive network. In addition, two clip-gauges were used to verify the crack opening displacement (CMOD), one on each face of the specimen. Two specimens were evaluated for each mix design to ensure the reproducibility of the results.

For the electrical measurements, a constant DC voltage of 10 V was applied to each specimen using a circuit equipped with a 1kΩ shunt resistor in series, as shown in Fig.  2 . A Keysight DAQ970 data acquisition system was utilized to measure the voltage across the resistor, allowing the calculation of the electrical resistivity of the samples through Ohm’s Law (Eqs.  1 – 2 ) and the subsequent determination of FCR using Eq.  3 , where  R  is the electrical resistance [Ω],  V  is the voltage [V],  i  is the electrical current [A],  A  is the electrode contact area with the cement matrix [cm²],  L  is the distance between the electrodes [cm],  ρ  and  ρ 0  are the electrical resistivity and its initial value before loading [Ω.cm], respectively.

In this equation,  y  is the dependent variable,  x  is the independent variable (time),  y 0  is the baseline constant,  A 1  and  A 2  are the pre-exponential amplitudes, and  t 1  and  t 2  are the decay time constants. This mathematical refinement allowed the subtraction of residual drift, effectively isolating the genuine electrical response caused only by mechanical behavior. Consequently, this procedure ensures a stable and reliable baseline, mitigating any polarization noise remaining after the initial 20-minute stabilization period. Finally, the splitting test results were then compared with the electrical data achieved to establish the sensing capabilities of the material.

Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) analysis was conducted to verify the action of PP fibers within the damaged regions after electromechanical tests. Observations were carried out using a Hitachi TM 3000 microscope on cross-sectional slices extracted from the specimens, focusing specifically on the internal crack walls. It should be noted that the resolution of the benchtop microscope utilized limits the observation to micro-scale features. Therefore, the carbon nanotubes are not visible in these micrographs, which focus exclusively on visualizing the PP fibers acting within the matrix.

sections.heading: Materials characterization
paragraphs: A TEM image obtained for the CNT particles is shown in Fig.  3 . It is possible to identify cylindrical nanostructures with a high aspect ratio, which is in good agreement with the specifications from the manufacturer, which specifies an average diameter of 9.5 nm and an average length of 1.5 μm. The micrographs show a dense network of nanotubes characterized by their sinuous morphology. The chemical composition and density determined for the cement are presented in Table  2 .

sections.heading: CNT dispersion
paragraphs: The visual evolution of CNT dispersion in aqueous solution as a function of sonication cycles is presented in Fig.  4 . Initially, at lower energy inputs (C1-C3), the presence of macroscopic clusters and a non-homogeneous distribution is evident, indicating that the electrostatic attraction between nanotubes due to van der Waals forces and hydrophobic effects have not yet been sufficiently overcome. As the number of cycles increases (C4-C8), a progressive darkening of the solution is observed, corresponding to the debundling of CNT agglomerations into smaller clusters and individual particles. At the final stages (C9-C10), the solution achieves a high degree of visual homogeneity, characterized by an opaque black color with no discernible sedimentation or suspended agglomerates.
Fig. 4 CNT dispersion evolution through increasing number of cycles

In sequence, Fig.  5  shows the UV-Vis spectroscopy results. For the first dispersion (D1), an analysis was performed for each cycle, revealing that the absorbance spectrum increases as the number of cycles advances, reaching its maximum value in the last cycle (C10). The absorbance spectra showed that all samples exhibit a characteristic peak around 250–300 nm, corresponding to the presence of individual carbon nanotubes [ 22 ], with a final value after the last cycle of approximately 1.2 a.u. Furthermore, it is possible to correlate the absorbance curves with the visual inspection presented before, revealing the evolution of CNT dispersion as the number of cycles increases.
Fig. 5 UV-Vis spectroscopy results of  a  all 10 cycles from dispersion D1 and  b  the final cycle for every performed dispersion

The comparison of the final cycle for each CNT dispersion reveals consistent behavior, with a characteristic absorbance of 1.2 a.u. (± 0.2). Following the homogenization of the individual dispersions into a single volume, the final solid content of the carbon nanotubes was measured to determine the process efficiency. To ensure reliability, the solid content of the dispersion was quantified in triplicate via mass loss analysis. The results indicated an average mass loss of 95.8% (± 0.2%), which corresponds to the evaporation of the aqueous phase. Consequently, the total solid content of the suspension was determined to be 4.2%. Given the initial 1:1 solid ratio between carbon nanotubes and superplasticizer, the final effective concentration of CNTs in the dispersion was established at 2.1%.

sections.heading: Bulk electrical resistivity
paragraphs: In the electrical resistivity curve presented in Fig.  6 , the cement/PP/CNT composites exhibit classic percolation behavior, where the addition of carbon nanotubes transforms the matrix from an insulating state into a conductive one. This was evidenced by fitting the Boltzmann equation. At the initial concentrations of 0.00% and 0.25%, the highest values are observed (around 100kΩ.cm), indicating that the nanotubes are insufficient to create an electrical network. However, the region between these concentrations indicates the percolation threshold, marked by a sharp drop in electrical resistivity. This visual conclusion is supported by a mathematical approach. According to the Power Law used in this study, the percolation threshold occurs exactly at a CNT content of 0.12%, using a critical exponent ( t ) of 2.22 that results in a R² of 0.99 for this dosage. In sequence, at the dosage of 0.50%, the material is set in the transition zone. This phenomenon indicates the establishment of a functional conductivity network, but with limited number and sparse conductive pathways that, potentially, make the electrical response highly sensitive to mechanical strain [ 5 ,  37 ,  38 ]. To conclude, the CNT contents of 0.75% and 1.00% are already within the conductive zone, where further increases in CNT content result in only a marginal reduction in resistivity, signaling that the system has reached a saturated conductive network.
Fig. 6 a  Electrical resistance curve of cement/PP/CNT composites and  b  linear fit of percolation threshold from Percolation Theory Power Law

sections.heading: Electromechanical behavior on damage detection
paragraphs: The correlation between mechanical performance and electrical signals was evaluated through splitting tests, aiming to identify the CNT concentrations capable of detecting crack initiation. These results can be found in Fig.  7 . Initially, the PP fibers act through crack-bridging, preventing a brittle failure and ensuring the specimen maintains enough structural integrity for the CNT network to register the damage signal and understand its efficiency for this application. For samples with 0.00% and 0.25% CNT, the fractional change in resistivity at the moment of failure was negligible, ranging between 0% and 1%, rendering these dosages ineffective for self-sensing applications. In contrast, concentrations from 0.50% to 1.00% CNT demonstrated a robust capacity to identify damage initiation through significant FCR variations as cracking progress. To better visualize the exact moment of crack initiation, the inset small graphs provide a magnified view of the initial electrical response up to 50% of FCR. The 0.50% CNT dosage exhibited the highest sensitivity, with FCR values reaching 125% and 500% at failure. This concentration falls within the electrical transition zone of the material, where the conductive network is sparse. Consequently, the change in resistivity is more sensitive to the physical disconnection of CNT, as the formation of a single crack can interrupt a significant portion of the available electrical pathways. In this context, the 0.50% dosage represents the lowest among the compositions studied to exhibit electrical sensitivity to damage in the cement/PP/CNT composites, showing an exponential jump in FCR that coincides with the peak mechanical load.

Although the non-linear fitting reduced the baseline drift from DC polarization, some noise remains in the electrical signal. This noise is primarily caused by the contact between the copper electrodes and the cement matrix. In the two-probe setup, small movements during the test can disturb the electrical contact, creating temporary instability. However, the overall FCR response remains clear enough to detect damage.
Fig. 7 Splitting test results and electromechanical correlation for  a  0.00CNT,  b  0.25CNT,  c  0.50CNT,  d  0.75CNT, and  e  1.00CNT samples

For higher concentrations of 0.75% and 1.00%, the maximum FCR achieved at failure was reduced, yielding values between 100% and 250% and 100%-150%, respectively. This suggests that a denser conductive network reduces relative sensitivity despite maintaining high overall conductivity. In these higher dosages, the current can be effectively rerouted through adjacent nanotube pathways as cracks open, which prevents extreme FCR spikes but ensures a more stable and predictable electrical response, as illustrated in Fig.  8 .
Fig. 8 Electrical response of cement/PP/CNT composites with different CNT concentrations

To explicitly correlate the physical crack propagation with the electrical resistivity changes, Fig.  9  presents the relationship between CMOD to FCR. This analysis corroborates the initial loading findings by demonstrating how the physical widening of the crack directly governs the continuous evolution of the electrical signal. For 0.00% and 0.25% CNT compositions, the fractional change in resistivity increases gradually as the crack opens, lacking a distinct change in the electrical signal for damage initiation. In contrast, for dosages of 0.50% CNT and above, a significant increase in FCR is noticed at low CMOD levels. These results confirm that the high sensitivity and damage detection capabilities previously discussed are directly linked to the response of the conductive network to crack opening. In this context, the CMOD data validates that while the 0.50% CNT dosage remains the most sensitive concentration, higher dosages (0.75% and 1.00%) provide a superior correlation for quantitative monitoring. Their denser carbon nanotube pathways within the cement matrix facilitate a more linear relationship between physical crack displacement and the electrical signal.
Fig. 9 Correlation between CMOD and FCR during electromechanical tests for  a  0.00CNT,  b  0.25CNT,  c  0.50CNT,  d  0.75CNT, and  e  1.00CNT samples

sections.heading: Microstructural analysis
paragraphs: SEM analysis was conducted to investigate the microstructural mechanisms provided by the PP fibers, which govern the mechanical stability of the composite during the electromechanical tests. Figure  10  presents the fracture surfaces and the interaction between the PP fibers and the cementitious matrix. The micrographs display the energy absorption mechanisms activated under tensile stress, specifically fiber debonding and pull-out. The images highlight distinct gaps at the fiber-matrix interface, channels left by debonded fibers, and empty voids resulting from complete fiber pull-out. These features demonstrate that the fibers undergo controlled damage opening rather than sudden rupture when the matrix cracks. Furthermore, the visual comparison confirms that the incorporation of 1.00% CNT does not hinder this behavior, as both matrices exhibit similar pull-out and debonding characteristics. This progressive interfacial failure mechanism is fundamental to dissipating energy and avoiding the inherent brittleness of the cement paste.
Fig. 10 SEM images of  a  0.00CNT [150x],  b  0.00CNT [1000x],  c  1.00CNT [150x], and  d  1.00CNT [1000x] cement/PP/CNT samples

Furthermore, Fig.  11  illustrates the robust crack-bridging effect exerted by the PP fibers across a well-defined damage. As the crack propagates during the splitting test, the randomly distributed fibers stretch across the fracture zone, effectively transferring the load between the separated faces. This bridging action controls the crack opening displacement and restricts rapid crack widening. By preventing catastrophic failure, the PP fibers ensure that the specimen maintains the necessary structural integrity throughout the loading process. This extended and controlled damage evolution is essential for the successful execution of the electromechanical tests, as it prevents instantaneous complete disconnection of the sample and provides the required timeframe for the internal conductive network to continuously register the piezoresistive response as structural damage progresses.
Fig. 11 SEM images of 1.00CNT samples showing crack-bridging control during electromechanical tests at  a  [150x] and  b  [1000x]

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: This study investigates the self-sensing capabilities of cement pastes incorporating multi-walled carbon nanotubes and polypropylene fibers. Based on the results achieved, the following conclusions can be drawn:

The implementation of an initial 20-minute polarization period combined with non-linear data fitting successfully mitigated electrical drift induced by DC. This methodology allowed the isolation of the true electrical response for crack initiation. The electrical percolation threshold of the composite was identified at 0.12% of CNT. The 0.50CNT dosage yielded the highest sensitivity for damage detection. Lower dosages (≤ 0.25%) were unable to provide measurable electrical responses to crack initiation. In contrast, higher concentrations (0.75% and 1.00%) formed denser networks that reduced relative sensitivity but provided a more linear relationship between crack displacement and the electrical signal. CNT combined with PP fibers creates a multifunctional composite. The crack-bridging capability of the PP fibers prevents sudden brittle failure, which is essential to enable the internal CNT network to continuously register damage evolution without immediate disconnection. This synergy validates the material as a reliable intrinsic sensor for SHM applications. The current findings are limited to the evaluation of localized crack formations induced by controlled tensile splitting tests under static DC stimuli. Future research must investigate the performance of these self-sensing cementitious composites under dynamic loading, multi-axial stresses, and varying environmental factors to fully validate their field applicability.
